title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pair_count = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z), the Mininet 10% holdout (20 tasks) that produced zero validator–emulator disagreements, and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating natural‑language intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises operational efficiency but raises safety concerns: incorrect or semantically invalid configurations can cause outages or violate policies. Prior work therefore recommends grounding and deterministic verification (generate→validate→repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. Yet the operational value of automated repair depends on (1) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the deployed generator and prompting policy, (2) validator coverage and fidelity, and (3) the repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. To measure the marginal effect of deterministic validation+repair on identical generator outputs, we preregistered a paired confirmatory study that fixes the initial generator output per task and compares applying that same candidate unchecked versus validating—and, if necessary, issuing one automated repair prompt to the same model.
sections.related_work: Empirical studies and surveys show LLMs produce factual errors and hallucinations across domains and that verifier‑assisted repair, retrieval grounding, and guarded agent architectures are plausible mitigations. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate intent→configuration feasibility but typically lack externally auditable, instrumented failure‑rate measurements. Red‑team audits and configuration‑brittleness studies document how tool descriptions, persona/history, and chaining can change agent behavior and safety outcomes. Our study addresses a specific gap identified in that literature: a preregistered, artifact‑grounded measurement isolating the marginal effect of deterministic repair on a fixed generator output.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. We preregistered study cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02: a paired design with n = 200 tasks (4 topology clusters × 50 tasks), one shared deterministic initial generation per task, and up to one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated by an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile CIs used 10,000 resamples with bootstrap_seed = 1729. The analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1.

Task bank, validator, and emulator. The task bank contains 200 machine‑checkable intent→configuration tasks that encode initial and expected final states plus workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group‑active minima) and required sequences. The primary deterministic checker enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). As preregistered, a Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator served as a secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to reveal validator blind spots.

Shared‑initial semantics and determinism reconciliation. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate that was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This design removes sampling variance across conditions so the paired contrast isolates the marginal effect of invoking the validator and of issuing the single allowed repair. We reconcile a potential ambiguity in the model configuration artifact: execution/model_configuration.json records the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and lists temperature as null; determinism for the primary estimand was achieved by adapter semantics rather than by asserting model‑internal sampling parameters. Deterministic_reconciliation.json and the execution provider audit fields (hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}; cache_miss_count = 200) demonstrate that exactly one model invocation per task produced the shared initial candidate and that the same candidate was reused across conditions. Thus the primary inferential contrast measures the effect of validation+repair on the identical generated output rather than the effect of multiple independent stochastic draws.

Repair policy, execution caps, and handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt to the same LLM when the primary validator reported violations; repaired candidates (if any) were re‑validated deterministically. The adapter enforced a model‑call cap of 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repairs). Missingness rules deterministically excluded pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure execution failures; contamination handling preplanned to exclude pairs with primary validator vs emulator disagreement. All decisions and seeds are recorded in the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed to completion under the frozen preregistration (start: 2026‑08‑30T11:50:34.530059Z; end: 2026‑08‑30T12:12:07.541650Z). Accounting artifacts show completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), maximum_model_calls = 400, and repair_calls_used = 0. Provider audit fields record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming single shared invocations per task.

Validator outcomes and paired inference. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200 (condition summary). The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0. The prespecified exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0, and the bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) is [0.0, 0.0]. Because there are no discordant pairs, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis cannot be evaluated on this sample.

Repair and contamination checks. No validator failures occurred and therefore no repair prompts were issued; secondary estimands (repair iterations, GVR‑introduced failures, model‑call cost per repair) are empty in the analysis artifacts. The Mininet randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) produced zero disagreements between the primary validator and the emulator in the executed sample.

Representative diagnostics. Per‑task validator traces confirm parsed_command_count matched required_command_count for representative tasks and show difficulty labels ("medium", "hard", "very_hard") and dependency patterns (make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change, rolling_access_vlan_migration), indicating the task bank exercised nontrivial workflow constraints despite all outputs satisfying the validator checks.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The degenerate paired outcome (no discordant pairs) is an artifact‑grounded observation: under the shared‑initial generation policy and the chosen model+prompting policy, the generator produced validator‑satisfying outputs for every task. That result is not evidence that repair is universally unnecessary; it precisely states that, on this curated workload and with the frozen shared‑initial semantics, there were no validator‑detectable failures for the GVR process to reduce. The paired design intentionally isolates the marginal effect of invoking the validator+repair on the identical candidate; it excludes gains achievable by re‑sampling the LLM or by using nonzero‑temperature sampling.

Statistical note on the degenerate paired case. With n10 = n01 = 0 the McNemar statistic is degenerate: the exact two‑sided p = 1.0 and bootstrap percentile CIs collapse to a point [0.0, 0.0] under the recorded resampling parameters (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). These numbers correctly reflect the data observed but provide no information about reductions that would be achievable against a nonzero baseline failure prevalence.

Methodological tradeoffs and operational implications. The shared_initial paired contrast offers high internal control but sacrifices the ability to estimate unconditional generator failure rates that arise when sampling diversity is admitted. For operational assurance, practitioners should first measure unconditional baseline validator failure prevalence under the intended production sampling/generation policy; if failures are rare, a single‑pass repair budget yields limited marginal safety returns and resources may be better directed to expanding validator fidelity, adversarial testing, or multi‑sample generation to surface latent failures. Conversely, when baseline failures are nontrivial, GVR with an appropriate repair budget and richer repair prompts can materially reduce validator‑detected errors.

Validator fidelity and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators codify an oracle of checks but can have blind spots for device idiosyncrasies or end‑to‑end data‑plane effects. The preregistered Mininet holdout acts as a practical independent detector; the executed 20‑task holdout produced zero disagreements, but the holdout selection seed is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle, creating a reproducibility gap for exact reconstruction of that draw.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), yielding a paired difference of 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0, and bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]. The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. The artifact‑grounded outcome clarifies that GVR’s marginal utility depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and validator coverage: when validator‑detectable failures are rare under the chosen generation policy, single‑step automated repair yields no measured benefit for those specific validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, adopt mixed sampling designs to estimate unconditional failure prevalence, expand validator fidelity and holdout emulation coverage (with labeled seeds), evaluate multiple models or ensembles, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets to characterize practical operational gains. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived under the preregistration id cited above for independent inspection.

Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Determinism reconciliation: execution/model_configuration.json lists the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and records temperature as null; determinism for the primary paired estimand was achieved by adapter semantics (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) that produced and reused a single shared initial candidate per task. Deterministic_reconciliation.json and provider audit fields demonstrate hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming single shared invocations per task. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized selection seed used to draw the Mininet 10% holdout is not present as a labeled artifact in the archive; this absence prevents exact deterministic reconstruction of the drawn holdout despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested. Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
